en: The Sūtra on the Nirgrantha’s Inquiry into the Meaning of Non-Self,
compiled by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Subject Nichō, a Grand Master of Buddhist Propagation (Xuánfàn Dàshī) who has been conferred the purple robe, together with the Vice Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù Shǎoqīng). At that time, the Nirgranthas and others, harboring divergent views and giving rise to doubts, sought out and went to those who understood the Mahāyāna.
Having arrived, he prostrated, joined his palms in reverence, and asked about the meaning of selflessness (*anātman*) so that his dullness and ignorance might be dispelled:
"Please reveal this for me as the Buddha has taught.

If it is said that there is no self in this body, then even that supreme self would not exist. Why then do we clearly perceive within the body such things as weeping and laughing, playing, anger, pride, jealousy, and double-tongued speech?"
Being unable to determine whether existence or non-existence prevails, I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will sever this doubt for me.
The one who understands the Mahāyāna said to the Nirgrantha:
“That supreme self which you previously clung to is certainly false.”
By what means is it called "existence," and by what means is it called "non-existence"?
Within these two, nothing at all can be apprehended.

If one takes one's own hair, nails, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, fat, marrow, intestines, stomach, hands, feet, and all other limbs of the body as the supreme self, and searches both internally and externally, what could possibly be found?
Then the Nirgrantha said to the wise man, "Because I possess only the fleshly eye, I am unable to see; others who possess the divine eye can see it.
The wise man replied:
"Furthermore, it cannot be seen even by the divine eye.
It possesses neither manifest color nor shape; since its intrinsic nature is empty, how could there be anything visible?
The Nirgrantha said:
"Is it certain that they do not exist?
The wise one replied:
"If you say they do not exist, why is it that we directly perceive such phenomena as crying and laughing arising from causes and conditions?"
"To say that it exists or to say that it does not exist— both are erroneous and contrary to the correct principle," said the Nirgrantha.
"If neither existence nor non-existence should be asserted, how is it that this body currently has a place where it dwells?"
The wise one said:
"There is not even the slightest portion of a perceived characteristic of that which abides.
The Nirgrantha replied:
"If there is no dwelling or attachment, it is identical to empty space.
The wise one said:
"As you have said, because it is like empty space."
The Nirgrantha said:
"If that is so, how should one dispel such states as weeping and laughing?
The wise man replied:
Within this meaning there are two kinds: first, the conventional (saṃvṛti), and second, the ultimate (paramārtha).

According to the conventional, there are such distinctions as self, other, life-principle (jīva), person (pudgala), individual (puruṣa), agent, experiencer, wealth, wife and children, relatives, and associates.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no such thing as one’s own life or the lives of others, nor even such matters as factions and their associates; furthermore, there are no characteristics of even the slightest differentiation.
From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), there is arising and ceasing, as well as the retribution of good and evil;
however, within the ultimate truth, there is no arising and ceasing, nor any retribution of good and evil.
That *tathatā* (suchness) is pure by its very nature; it is without afflictions, without defilement, and without even the act of cognition, being quiescent from the beginning.
This is called the self-nature of *tathatā*.
To further clarify this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"The conventional and the ultimate truth— These two kinds shall now be explained.
The conventional is worldly phenomena; The ultimate is unsurpassed."
Sentient beings rely upon the conventional, whereby their afflictions increase;
dwelling long in saṃsāra, they do not understand the ultimate dharma.
Because they rely upon the conventional, they give rise to pervasive conceptualizations regarding self and others.
Giving rise to conceptual discrimination and doubt, they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
Those foolish worldlings are oppressed for a long time;
since they do not cultivate the causes for transcendence, how could they know the principle of liberation?
Fools constantly rely upon the phenomena of arising and ceasing in the world;
they rush through the five destinies, continuing on without interruption.
Because they do not realize the ultimate truth, they lack the essential means for extinguishing suffering.
Revolving through the cycle of saṃsāra, they are like silkworms binding themselves with their own cocoons.
Just as the sun and moon rotate without rest,
so too do sentient beings come and go within the three realms of existence.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, changing and shifting from moment to moment;
one should distance oneself from worldly dharmas and seek the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
This applies even to those dwelling among the devas, as well as the gandharvas and others.
They cannot escape impermanence; these are all merely worldly fruits.
Even yakṣas, bhūtas, and other spirits who have attained the accomplishments of vidyādharas cannot avoid falling into the evil destinies; these are all merely worldly fruits.
Śakra and the Wheel-Turning Kings, though their meritorious retributions are peerless, cannot avoid falling into the animal realm; these are all merely worldly fruits.
The pleasures of the five desires of humans and devas must certainly be renounced.
Regarding that bodhicitta, one should constantly observe it with wisdom.
Its intrinsic nature is without attachment; all things are entirely empty.
Transcending all conceptual proliferation—this is the characteristic of bodhicitta.
Neither hard nor soft, neither hot nor cold,
neither tangible nor graspable— such is the characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Neither long nor short, neither round nor square.
Neither subtle nor coarse—this is the characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Neither white nor red, neither black nor yellow;
neither shape-color nor manifest-color—this is the characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Neither form nor radiance, neither movement nor bondage,
abiding like space— this is the characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Beyond conceptual thought and observation, it is not the domain of non-Buddhists.
In accord with Prajñā, this is the characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Without likeness and without counterpart, without equal and eternally quiescent,
its self-nature fundamentally unmoving— this is the characteristic of the bodhicitta.
Like a mass of foam or a floating bubble, like a magical illusion or a mirage, it is without self and impermanent; all things are not solid.
This body is like a fragile earthen vessel, empty yet seemingly full.
Associated with the three poisons, they are ultimately empty and non-existent.
Like the moon amidst the clouds, it does not appear for even a moment;
through the profound *prajñā*, one realizes that conditioned phenomena are like illusions.
The world of sentient beings and the receptacle world—everything is like a dream;
arising from the conceptualization of one’s own mind, that mind itself is also like a dream.
If a person relies on correct reasoning and cultivates through wisdom, [they will realize this].
Abandoning all hindrances and defilements, one swiftly attains the unsurpassed path.
This most excellent Prajñā is praised by all Buddhas;
the wise, having carefully deliberated, diligently seek the unsurpassed Dharma.
Having abandoned the faults of the conditioned and realized the supreme virtues of the true and eternal,
through this liberation, all things are free from defilement and attachment.
At that time, the assembly of non-Buddhists, having heard this, gave rise to joy.
Skillfully observing and removing doubt, one attains the wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
*The Sūtra on the Questions of the Nirgrantha Regarding the Meaning of Non-Self*
